Mr. W. G. ERNST (Queens-Lunenburg) presented the third and fourth reports of the select standing committee on marine and fisheries as follows:
Third Report
Your committee has had under consideration Bill No. 17, an Act to amend the Fisheries Act, 1932. Representations in the form of briefs have been submitted by the different interests concerned in the legislation contemplated, and a statement of the policy of the department has been made to the committee on the matter. After consideration, your committee is of the opinion that the public interest, as a whole, would not best be served by the passing of the proposed legislation.
Your committee, therefore, has agreed to report, on division, that the necessity for the amendment to the Fisheries Act, 1932, as contained in Bill No. 17, has not been proven to the satisfaction of your committee and should not be passed.
Fourth Report
Your committee has had under consideration the following resolution, referred to your committee by the house on Wednesday, February 6th:-
_ "That,' in the opinion of this house, in the interests of the fishermen of Nova Scotia, no permits should be granted on renewed with those who own and operate beam trawlers in the province of Nova Scotia."
Your committee has agreed to report that, whereas the royal commission on price spreads and mass buying has investigated the subject matter of the said resolution and made a report thereon, which may be the subject of discussion and consideration by parliament, your committee is of the opinion that no useful purpose would be served by further investigation of the said matter by your committee at the present session of parliament.

Right- Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, I submit that the
motion is out of order having regard to the terms of the standing order to which reference has been made. The hon. gentleman has just sent me a copy of his proposal. In looking at standing order 31, I think it is quite clear that a motion under this standing order must relate to a matter that is of recent occurrence and must not revive discussion on a matter that has been discussed. May I observe first that this is not a matter of recent occurrence.
Secondly, may I point out that the hon. gentleman suggests that it creates a situation which endangers the peace. That is a matter over which this parliament has not control. As I pointed out yesterday, it is a matter solely within the jurisdiction of the province and of the municipality which is created by the province.
Lastly, if there is any grievance which the hon. gentleman has, he has adequate opportunity for the airing of those grievances at the appropriate time when the house is moved into committee of supply.
I think, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the matter is not within the rule but comes within the exceptions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whether or
not this motion is in order depends upon two or three points. First of all, it must be a specific matter and of- recent occurrence. Second, it must be of such urgency that it would require to be dealt with immediately. I contend that this is a specific matter and of recent occurrence, it having developed within the last day or two. I contend also that it is of such importance that the government should deal with it at this particular time. The government may take the position that the main-

taining of order is a matter for the city of Vancouver and the province of British Columbia but the government has been asked for assistance in maintaining order and to that extent the government enters into the question. If further disturbances occur the government will be asked for further assistance and consequently this matter very definitely concerns the government. Outside of the broad implications of the whole question I believe that for these reasons the matter should be discussed in the house.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE TO DISCUSS THE SITUATION IN VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Before ruling on this matter I should like to thank the hon. member who is responsible for this motion for having the courtesy to let me have a copy of it prior to the opening of the house, thus affording me an opportunity of giving some consideration to this important matter. I only wish that my duties were so simple that I could leave the question of urgency to be settled by the house, but unfortunately the rules place the duty upon the Speaker of deciding this matter. The question of urgency is covered by subsection (3) of standing order 31, which reads:
He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to Mr. Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house.
The question of urgency must for the moment be settled by me, although according to a precedent established before the recess my decision in the matter can be overruled by the house. I agree that the matter is of tremendous importance and urgency but I cannot agree with the proposer, Mr. Maclnnis, that the matter dealt with has arisen within the last day or two. The gravity of the situation may have increased recently but the events referred to are not of recent origin. The events referred to in the motion first happened when the men left the relief camps some time around April 10th last. To bring this motion within standing order 31 the matter proposed to be discussed must be of recent origin. May, page 227, as quoted in paragraph 240 of Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms has this to say:
A motion under this standing order must be restricted to a single specific matter of recent occurrence;
I find that this motion does not come within that authority. All hon. members are aware that while this matter was not discussed formally in debate it was covered pretty fully by a statement made yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I should like to quote one or two paragraphs from that state-

Unemployment Relief Camps
ment. I refer the house to page 2922 of Hansard of May 21 where the Prime Minister is quoted as follows:
I have drafted a communication to the premier of British Columbia in which I have endeavoured to point out that if the province fails in its duty to prevent a condition of chaos and anarchy arising, if they fail in their duty to maintain law and order in the province of British Columbia, it will only be because they have not availed themselves of the opportunity of requesting the federal government to lend them such assistance as may be required for that purpose, for until that is done any action on the part of this dominion would he wholly illegal and would be a compromising of our own position with those who may themselves be violating the law.
I direct the attention of the house to the last part of that statement. The Prime Minister continues:
The differences and difficulties, whatever they may be, the federal government will be glad to consider with the provincial government, but it is a condition precedent to any such action that law and order be maintained by those who are responsible for it, and if they are unable to do so that they call upon the federal government for such assistance as will enable them to do so.
I quote those particular paragraphs because of the following which appears at page 248 of May, Thirteenth Edition:
Motions have also been ruled out of order when it appeared that the administrative responsibility of the government was not involved, or that there had not been any departure from the ordinary administration of the law.
The precedents quoted at the bottom of the same page are as follows:
Motions have been held out of order as the subject sought to be raised was within the cognizance of the parliament of Northern Ireland. 154 H.C. Deb. 5 s 1894; the Irish Free State, 152 ib. 2435; 154 ib. 529; a matter for the local police, 120 ib. 261; a labour dispute in which the government was under no obligation to intervene, 162 ib. 33; 166 ib. 450.
The maintenance of law and order is admittedly a matter for the provincial and municipal authorities. The subject matter of this motion is therefore, in my opinion, provincial, not federal, and the motion is on the authority just referred to, not in order. I should have pointed out previously that the statement of the Prime Minister already referred to makes it quite clear that the government has been aware for some time of the matters referred to in the motion. For some weeks past the federal officials have been kept advised of the state of local affairs by the Mayor of Vancouver and the Premier of British Columbia. These are further facts which induce me to rule that this motion does not come within the authority first quoted. I
am also of the opinion that the matter is one of departmental administration and not one for legislative action by this parliament. For these various reasons and above authorities I am therefore constrained to rule that this motion is not in order.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, May 21, consideration in committee of Bill No. 63, to create employment by public works and undertakings throughout Canada and to authorize the guarantee of certain railway equipment securities-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)- Mr. Morand in the chair.
On schedule A, item 9-Harbours and rivers generally, $2,500,000.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Last night the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) directed attention to statements made by the Minister of Public Works that certain information and details would be forthcoming concerning the
Public Works Program

amounts the government wants to appropriate, $2,500,000 for public works to be undertaken under the item of harbours and rivers. Looking at page 2817 of Hansard of 16th April I find that answering a question put by my right hon. leader the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) said:
I am certainly in a position to give details on every item.
Now we are on this item of $2,500,000 which is to be allocated and spent in the various ports of Canada. It is all very well to say we might appropriate a couple of hundred thousand for Quebec and so much for Ontario and so much for other provinces.
What the people want to know, and what we as representatives of those people want to know, is how this money is to be qpent, where it is to be spent, and for what purposes. It has always been the privilege of hon. members not to vote any large amounts of money without first knowing where they are to be spent. Last night the minister had the deputy minister in front of him, a man who has been in the department for twenty-two years and who is throroughly familiar with the facts. Then, he must have received help from his officials in Quebec and elsewhere in the province who would be in a position to tell him the various amounts required which would go to make up whatever portion of the $2,500,000 is to be spent in the province of Quebec.
Last night I made special reference to certain public works in which I am vitally interested. The minister told me he expected to be able to attend to some of those works, but he gave no specific indication as to which works would be undertaken. I am still hoping that something will be done. The people throughout the country want to know in what places in the province of Quebec the works are to be carried out, and what sums of money will be spent. I believe all hon. members from the Atlantic to the Pacific are keenly interested, and it is our privilege as members of this chamber to have precise information such as the minister promised to give _ on April 16, when the bill was under discussion. I await the answer of the minister.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I believe it is only fair to say that in addition to these works I am receiving from members suggestions every day as to works needed in their respective constituencies. From time to time these are being referred to engineers for reports. While we have now a total of $9,417,792 there are some projects in respect of which we have no report, indicating the amount of the expenditures required. Therefore I believe it is fair to say that the requests already in and those which will come in will exceed $10,000,000. I believe every hon. member will agree that it is impossible at this time to give a complete list of the particular works which will be done, their locations and the amount of money required. I am willing to give all the information available, but I regret I cannot now say in what amounts this money will be expended. In this regard I am not taking a position different from that taken by my predecessor in respect of similar votes. I have before me Hansard for 1929, and at page 2047, dealing with harbours and rivers generally, repairs and improvements amounting to $80,000 for the province of Nova Scotia, I find the following:
Mr. Short: I should like to ask the minister on what he proposes to expend this $80,000 and in what sections of Nova Scotia?
Mr. Elliott: I can only tell the hon. member where the general vote was expended and how it was expended last year. This is to meet the ordinary maintenance charges made up of several small items, many of which can be foreseen at the present time.
Then at page 170 of Hansard for 1930 appears the item:
Nova Scotia-Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $100,000.
And the following discussion:
Mr. Ernst: May I ask, as a matter of information only, whether this amount of $100,000 is based upon the previous estimate of the requirements, and if so, what expenditure is contemplated and in what places?

Public Works Program
Mr. Elliott: The estimate is based upon what the engineer thinks the requirements will be in connection with works which should properly come out of the general vote.
Mr. Ernst: Are details given?
Mr. Elliott: No. We do not know, as my hon. friend will readily understand, what works will have to be done perhaps due to freshets and that sort of thing that may occur even after this vote is passed.
Mr. Ernst: It is a sort of emergency fund.

speechtext:

day which makes it perfectly clear that the extract he has read relating to something which occurred in 1929 has no application to this vote whatever. speechtext: Can the minister give me one instance?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I cannot give
an instance offhand, but I think my hon. friend's recollection will confirm my statement. Let us take an example. A petition comes in for the repairing of a wharf. The engineer visits the locality and finds that the wharf is in a very poor state of repair and that because of a change in conditions in that particular area the wharf would be better located a mile down the shore. In some cases it has been found that better service can be provided by such a move. The construction of that wharf would be new construction in the technical sense of the word but I submit that a fair interpretation of the term "repairs and improvements" would permit the inclusion of such a work provided it improved the facilities of a particular harbour. What difference does it make whether it is the reconstruction of a defunct structure or the construction of an entirely new work? I assure my hon. friend that my information is reliable when I say that entirely new works are constructed by the Public Works Department every year under the vote for repairs and improvements.
There is a further difference between this vote and the one referred to by my hon. friend. The votes to which he has referred were ordinary supply votes, and the rule, with which I have no quarrel, is very properly laid down that with respect to such votes there shall be as definite and as specific information furnished as is possible. I would direct the attention of my hon. friend to the
Public Works Program

title of this bill, which is, " An act to create employment by public works." This bill is to relieve unemployment, and I think it is distinct from the ordinary supply vote. Works will be constructed where needed and where relief to unemployment can be afforded, and perhaps a little more latitude is given than would be given in connection with an item in a regular supply bill.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The committee is endeavouring to ascertain what is to be done with this $2,500,000 vote, but we do not seem to have made any headway. I should like to know why my hon. friend included an item for harbours and rivers generally when the old item of repairs and improvements would have covered this one. What was the idea of making a change? Why should the minister depart from what he said yesterday? The change was made to enable him to put in entirely new works with respect to which, during this session of the committee, he does not propose to disclose any information. That is apparently the reason; otherwise he would tell us.	.
Then he goes on to say that this is a public works construction act and differs from the ordinary estimates, and in that regard the Minister of Railways last night urged this contention: How can we tell until the item is passed what will be the details of the works to which it will be applied? That was the argument of the Minister of Railways last night, and he waxed warm over it in an endeavour to help out the Minister of Public Works-and he helped him out to the extent of taking up half an hour of the committee's time and putting the matter further back at the end of that time than it had been when we started. Let me read to the committee the explanation of the Minister of Railways with regard to No. 5, canals, repairs and improvements, $750,000. If he has forgotten it he will find it at page 2854. I asked this question:
Can the minister give no more definite statement as to how this amount of 50,000 is to be allocated than wliat he has just given?
His answer was:
Yes, I can give a good deal-
Good-bye; I see he is leaving.

speechtext: Let me assure my hon. friend I am not going out because of fear, but I must see someone outside.

Yes, I can give a good deal, but I am watching the clock rather anxiously and I do not wish to delay the bill. Let me give an example.

That was when they were pressing to get this through by six o'clock.
We are counting on doing the work not absolutely but approximately as this is given. As regard's the Murray canal,-
I want the minister to listen carefully to this. I really thought that his department had these details about as accurately as any department in the government, but the following are the details which the Minister of Railways gave with regard to this schedule when we were discussing the matter a month ago- and the Minister of Public Works had his estimates in as good shape a month ago as the Minister of Railways had. The Minister of Railways went on to say:
As regards the Murray canal, the estimate of my engineers is $3,750. Others are as follows:
Ontario-St. Lawrence canals....	$ 31,000
Prescott elevato*	 170.000
Quebec canals (about)	 147,000
Rideau canal	 20,000
St. Peter's canal	 8,000
Sault Ste. Marie canal	 1,900
Trent canal	 30,000
Welland canals	 300,000
What is there in the minister's argument that he cannot give estimates for the items that make up the amounts in these schedules, on the ground that it is a public works construction bill? The Minister of Railways gave items a month ago showing how his $750,000 was made up. He said, quite properly, "We are counting on doing the work not absolutely but approximately." We asked the Minister of Public Works yesterday, whether, out of this $2,500,000, he could not give us some idea in regard to some of the things to be done, and he told us he could not. He will not disclose one item. That, I say, is not treating the committee fairly. He cannot convince the committee that he does not know where he will spend any of that $2,500,000. If he does not know now, though he was prepared to put this bill through a month ago, when does he think he will know?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The only thing with regard to which I quarrel with my friend in connection with this is the repeated assertion that for some ulterior reason I am endeavouring to keep back from the committee some information which it should have. That is the only thing I resent all through his remarks. I say to him that that is not well founded. I have no complaint whatever as to the way in which the committee has treated me on former occasions, but this occasion is somewhat different from previous ones. Let me say to my hon. friend with respect to the works which we knew definitely we had to undertake, that all of these were provided for in the regular estimates. We had the information with regard to these; we had the reports of the engineers and made our decision. Since this information has been accumulated, these requests have been coming in. I tell my hon. friend again as clearly, candidly and firmly as I can that we have not made a decision as to where any portion of this $2,500,000 is to be expended, as to what amount is to be expended in any province or as to any allocation of it. I think he will agree that it would be impossible to do so until the information is complete, and also for the very reason which he gave himself on two occasions with respect to a much smaller item when all he could do was to refer to similar expenditures made in the previous year. I have given just the same information.
Again, all I can say is that we do not lenow; we have not made a decision, and the reason we have not made it is that the information is not complete. We cannot make a decision until the information is complete; from time to time additional information will come in and we will undertake works in the light of the information that comes in then. I dc not know that I can add anything more. We have threshed this over and over again. If my hon. friend insists upon asking for information with respect to which I have stated my position, I cannot help it.
With regard to the information given by the Department of Railways and Canals respecting the $750,000, again my hon. friend would be as consistent as he is now if he insisted upon knowing at just what point along those canals a certain amount of money was to be spent. The items are simply a breaking up of the big item. They say: On a certain canal we propose to spend a certain amount, but no details are given as to the exact places and the exact amounts.
Again I submit to my hon. friend that this is a measure to provide money for the relief of unemployment and for the improvement of our harbours and rivers, and it must be left elastic in order that we may meet the emergencies of the works, whether they be simply repairs or improvements or new structures such as have been constructed out of the general vote in years gone by. I do not think I can give my hon. friend any more information.

As regards the argument
that in respect of a less amount we were unable to give the full details, when the minister is spending $2,500,000 plus the items that are already in the estimates, he ought to give a little more information than if he were spending only a few thousand dollars The minister has in a very ingenious way let the cat out of the bag. The estimates were tabled, I understand, about January 29; that is a considerable time ago, before most of the damage due to spring freshets could possibly have occurred, to say nothing of their having been known and reported to the department. Surely since then the department must have

There is the discussion, and I want to take issue with the minister, along the same lines as the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott). Here we have a special bill, we have a special amount. The title of the bill states that it is relative to unemployment. The preamble says it is for the purpose of accelerating the recovery of trade and industry to more normal conditions, and:
Whereas in pursuance of the said act there are dominion public works throughout Canada in process of construction amounting approximately to thirty million dollars; and whereas employment can be further stimulated by the undertaking of works and projects mentioned in the schedule hereto to supplement the works authorized by The Public Works Construction Act, 1934: and whereas it is in the national interest that such works and projects should be undertaken:
Now if it is in the national interest that those works should be undertaken we, the representatives of the people, have the right to know where and in what amounts this large sum is to be allocated and where the works are going to be done. I grant that in the regular estimates you have items specified for each district and each place, amounts of 850,000, 860,000, 8125,000 as the case may be, and then at the end there is put for the province, $50,000 or 8100,000 to take care of contingencies and unforeseen expenses, repairs and improvements, and if in regard to that the minister should give the answer he has given to-day I would be ready to accept it. But here we have an amount of $2,500,000 for harbours and rivers generally; a blank cheque, giving carte blanche to the minister. I am not so much afraid of him, because I think he is fair and honest, and his officials are. But we are getting near the time of an election, and as an amount was put in last year to cover a purpose, very likely the same thing will do the trick this year. What will happen is that in some districts where it will be more advantageous to carry on works than in another district where the work is more needed, the government will authorize such work by day labour and under the supervision of a given man. I have in mind certain necessary work in my district. Is the minister going to tell me that these works are not going to be done? I would like to know if they are, because they are necessary, and I do not want it to happen that if it is more advantageous for the government or their friends, or to help any given man in any territory, this money will go there rather than to the places which are vitally interested in getting ameliorations and betterments which they have been longing for for many years. Here we have the government placing this amount at its own disposal and at the disposal of any department-because this money can be entrusted to any minister of the government to spend without the members representing the various constituencies and the country at large knowing where and how and in what manner the amount is going to be spent.
The minister did not qualify his answer at all, he said he would give the information. At page 2817 when this item was under discussion before recess the minister stated in answer to the leader of the opposition:
I am certainly in a position to give details on every item.
Well, this is the item, 82,500,000, on which members of this house have been pleading with the minister and the government for some little information; at least to have a specific amount for each province, and I would say each district in each province, and why the money is going to be spent. If the minister does not give the information it just resolves itself into this, that the government are not satisfied with what they have put in the main estimates, not satisfied with what they already have at their disposal. They have not made use of the whole $40,000,000 which was voted by a similar bill last year; I am told they have only spent about S6,000,000 of it. They are going to have at their disposal the balance of last year's vote and we are to be forced to vote more in this bill, with the result that between now and election time the government will be able at random, to suit the convenience of any candidate or any member, to give to this district or that any amount of money without any responsibility and without the safeguards with which in the old days and up to the present time the moneys of the people have been appropriated and voted for such expenditures.
This bill is quite different from the main estimates; it is a new departure, to relieve unemployment and accelerate recovery. The minister must have had reports from his officials and must be in a position to say where the works and projects mentioned in the preamble are. I think we should at least have from the minister information as to how much each province is going to get and each district; for instance in the province of Quebec how much is going to be appropriated to the district of Montreal, how much to the district of Quebec, the district of Chicoutimi, the district of Three Rivers, and the same for the province of Ontario, the maritime provinces, British Columbia and the other
Public Works Program

western provinces. I think we are not treating the government unfairly in asking for such information. Last year when a similar bill came up we had the various projects itemized and numbered from one to a couple of hundred, and then there was a special vote along the same lines as this one. We objected, I did for one, because sufficient details were ' not given. Are we to let the same thing be repeated this year? Why did not the minister use the same phraseology, the same form and detail and schedule as last year? As the hon. member for West Middlesex pointed out yesterday, what is very likely to happen next year, if perchance this government should be here-I do not think it will be, let us hope not-is that it will bring in only one item for the whole sum to be spent for public works by every department of the government. The minister says that his engineers report about 900 requests from certain provinces, but he must realize that hon. members know where some of those moneys will be spent. We know there are certain districts where repair* are most needed and where new construction, which the minister has admitted will be done under the measure, is required. He has requests before him, and he must know where the works are to be carried out. Why not let the committee have information as to these various amounts? For instance, let the minister advise the committee as to the largest amount, if he does not wish to give all the details. I understand there may be some expenditures of $1,000 or SI,500 and that there might be some difficulty in giving details, but if there are big projects to be undertaken in any province then the minister in justice to himself, to the government and to the country at large ought to give the details.

I have only a word or

In the old days we could not spend an amount over $1,000 without an item appearing in the estimates; items under $1,000 were included in a general vote. No expenditure over $5,000 could be made except by calling for tenders. This amount has since been raised to $15,000 and we are now voting blank cheques. Parliament has upheld this new procedure and I have nothing more to say about it.
As far as my own constituency is concerned I am making no objection to any expenditures which might be made there. However, I must say that in every case where work has been done it has been merely repair work. There is one exception, the new wharf which was constructed at Black Cape. There was a difference of opinion as to where this wharf should be located, whether at Hewatson's Point or Woodsmen Beach, but this was left to the engineers to decide. I do not like the minister to try to put forth the impression that this money is being expended for the relief of unemployment when in fact it is being expended simply for the benefit of the friends of the government. I doubt if during the last five years more than five per cent of the money expended has been paid to Liberals, those who carried out the contracts and the workmen generally were friends of the party in power. The minister himself admitted this last year and the same procedure was followed when we were in power. I do not object to that but I want to correct the impression that these works are for unemployment relief when in fact they are merely for the benefit of the party friends in each locality. I am receiving letters every day from people in the different parishes in my constituency asking if such and such a work is to be done. I cannot give them any information, all I can say is that under the present parliamentary procedure the last man to know about what is happening in a constituency is the opposition member representing that constituency. speechtext:
Each year the
Department of Labour determines a fair schedule of wages for all classes of labour on public works in different parts of the country. They vary from one end of Canada to the other. That schedule is sent to the Public Works department and is made a part of the contract for the particular work; and more than that, the schedule is posted on the work that is being carried on, so that the employees engaged on that work have access to it.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It varies with each district too, does it not?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It may. The
employee can consult the list that is posted on the work and ascertain whether he is being paid according to the schedule that has been adopted. From time to time inspections are made of the contractors' books to see that this is carried out, and if any complaint is made that a contractor does not observe the provisions of the contract and does not pay the wages provided by the schedule, an inspector is sent on and he is forced to do so. In some instances, after the contractor has been paid in full and an injustice of that

Public Works Program
kind has been discovered and, as the saying is, he has been put on the carpet, he is made to go back and pay the deficiency to all employees. Let me assure my hon. friend that every possible effort is made by the government to see that a high standard of wages is maintained. It is made a part of the contract and the contractor must give his employees some means of knowing what the schedule is. He is checked up and forced to comply strictly with the provision.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I know that many evasions
have taken place in connection with these contracts so far as fair wages are concerned. My object now is to find out what machinery the department will use to see that the fair wage clauses are observed. Do they wait for complaints to come in, or do inspectors from his department or the Labour department go round and see that the clauses are strictly enforced?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
There are two
checks in that regard. The Department of Public Works has its own inspector on the work for supervision, and he keeps in touch with what is going on; and the Department of Labour regularly sends a member of its staff to visit public works to consult with the men and find out the conditions and whether there are any grievances.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: With reference to patronage, I raised the question a day or two ago and I am forced to bring it up again after what has been said this afternoon. Can we take it as a fact that in public works of this kind people can be employed only from a patronage list?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
So far as this department is concerned there is no patronage list for the employment of labour on contracts. That is entirely for the contractor himself. I have no doubt that where a public work is carried on those representing any political party or organization may go to the contractor and ask to have certain men employed. I do not know that we can prevent that, nor do I think that we should. I do not know that it would be right to prevent my hon. friend in the city of Winnipeg from going to a contractor who has a contract for a building and saying, "I know A.B. or C.D.; he is a good workman and is out of employment; can you not give him a chance? Can you not find a place for him?" Surely there is nothing wrong about that, even though it is done by a member of parliament or any other person or organization. After
all, however, the contractor must decide whom he will employ, and we exercise no control in that regard.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That is all right as stated by the minister. I have no objection to anyone going to a contractor and submitting a name or names to him. I have not done that myself because it creates trouble for the one who does it.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: He has a perfect right to do it.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Yes, but the man is foolish who does it because it only makes trouble for h|imself and he becomes an employment agent. I refuse to be an employment agent; I would rather attend to my duties as a member of parliament. What I am trying to point out-and I think the minister is skating on thin ice-is that in certain parts of the country when men want work they are obliged to go to political organizations. I do not say that this is done with the connivance or even with the knowledge of the Department of Public Works or of the minister; but somehow or other, when these contracts are let, it is known to the political party in power-as a matter of fact I have on file letters to that effect- and persons seeking employment have to go to Conservative headquarters before their names are placed on the eligible list. I object to that and I do not care what party is in power. I say that a man should be able to get a job irrespective of his political convictions, and I think that on this matter the minister ought to make a pronouncement from his seat in this house. He should protest against that practice and state that so far as he and the government are concerned they object to any of these positions being handled through any political party. It is a very simple matter. The minister can make that statement on the floor of the house and assure us that if such a thing is being done, or if it is brought to his attention, the government will put an end to it. I do not know whether he is prepared to go so far as to get up in the house and state that the government object to any party having anything whatever to do with the provision of eligible lists for submission to contractors.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I want my hon. friend (Mr. Heaps) to understand that I did not advocate anything in particular. I wished to impress upon the house the change that had taken place in conditions. I wanted to show that we had got away from the old parliamentary practice of many years ago, when parliament controlled public expenditures and not one dollar
2992	COMMONS
Public Works Program
could be voted by the house unless ministers of the crown had first of all indicated how the money was going to be spent. That is what I advocated. We have had two classes of expenditure in this country during the last five years. One has been in regard to unemployment relief. As far as I can learn unemployment relief expenditures have been among both political parties; 'both Liberals and Conservatives have been employed; but when the matter was a purely departmental work given out in the usual course of business by the party in power, of course the old method was followed that the government stood by its friends as it expected its friends to stand by it. It has appointed its friends to control these works. That has always been done in Canada and will be done for a long time to come, even if our friends to my left ever reach office.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I want to add a few words along the line of those just uttered by the hon. member for Bonaventure. When I was on the other side of the house and when there were any public works to be undertaken in my district, when a superintendent of works was appointed, in each case I used to give him instructions to employ as far as possible all people, Liberals and Conservatives alike, that were most in need of work to earn money. I know in many places there was no complaint at all and those who were in need of work, Liberals and Conservatives, got it. But at the present time I may tell the committee that in many places where works have been carried on, for instance at Ste. Anne de Beaupre, Pointe au Pic and otheT places, only Conservatives were employed and those who were known to be Liberals were turned down. In some places I know of, for instance at St. Irenee, only Conservatives were employed to do some work and earn a certain amount of money while Liberals were in need and other people whose party affiliations we do not know, did not get anything to do. The Tories got it all; there was a wrangle among them and those who fought the hardest got the most.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister who is the owner of an island which appears on the plan which I hold in my hand. It is the little circle that the minister will see at the mouth of the Riviere du Chene at St. Eustache, in the county of Two Mountains.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I do not know who owns the island.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I am surprised that the minister does not know because it is in the

constituency of the Postmaster General and some dredging has been done there. What amount of dredging has been done there?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: As I recall the matter, my hon. friend asked for a return which was brought down and delivered to him which gives all the particulars of the work carried on there in the past and must contain the item to which he now refers. I have not a copy of the return before me, so I cannot speak from memory as to what the expenditure was.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: But on the return that I have and which has been carefully combed, there is no hair; the dandruff only has been left. This is why it is so embarrassing to try to get complete information. According to the return given by the minister, a sum of $32,000 was expended there for dredging and filling. May I ask the minister whether this is all the money that was spent there or whether an additional amount was spent by the Quebec provincial government for the same purpose?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: My recollection is that the Quebec government did not make any contribution to the dredging to which my hon. friend refers. It made a contribution to some works but not to this particular one.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Some money has been spent there. We complained the other day about the Toronto tunnel, but this is one of the greatest extravagances of this government. Here we have an island with-i out a name and in the vicinity we see the church and properties belonging to Georges Paquin and E. Charles Girard. There is another property belonging to L'Oeuvre et Fabrique de St. Eustache. Then there is an ice shed and St. Eustache cemetery. There is a property near there in the name of the PosL master General and next to him is a property belonging to Madame Aube. I understand the island belongs to the Postmaster General. Let us see how shallow the water is around it. The readings of depth are given as: 1-7 feet, 2-1 feet, 1-2 feet, 1-9 feet, 2-1 feet, 1-8 inches, 3-1 feet, 2-3 feet, 2-7 feet, three-tenths of a foot, 1-7 feet, 1-2 feet, three-tenths of a foot. This is the channel around the island and the government has spent $32,000 for that.
There is worse than that. I am told by reliable people that that money has been spent to improve the estate of the Postmaster General and some excavation has been made. On the plan which is not signed but

Public Works Program
which comes with return reference 256, sessional paper ,No. 350, there appears this description :
Area of loose rock cleaned by hand. The big boulders on this shoal were dynamited, and' all stones and boulders wheelbarrowed, one part on adjacent island, other part on shore opposite. This shoal was cleaned to low water level in 1934 by day labour.
I would ask the Minister of Public Works -and perhaps I will give him some inside information as to what is going on in his department-whether it is not true that the dredging was the digging of that shallow water of less than one foot in some places in order to increase it to three-that was the answer given-to improve the navigation facilities for small craft around the island belonging to the Postmaster General. That is the first point. There was quite a heavy expenditure on that and there were numerous complaints from the electors of that constituency of Two Mountains that there was enough of that dredging. Then there was some filling. All the rocks and boulders that had been brought to the island to make it a fortress were taken from the island into the stream again, and that was filling. That was an expenditure of $32,000. Why is the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Simpson) smiling? If an hon. member of my own party were doing a thing like that, I would denounce him instead of approving of his action by my smile. I wonder whether there is a single elector in my hon. friend's constituency who would approve such extravagant waste of money as that at the expense of the country for a minister of the crown. What surprises me is this: there is in this big file only one mention of the Postmaster General, stating that he wishes the work to be done at the earliest opportunity. It was such a scandalous work that the rocks had to be taken from the island and thrown again into the stream. Of course no one is surprised at that when one considers that S20.000 has been given as pure graft for a man who had invented that famous postal box made of a stovepipe. Well sir. the postage has been increased one cent, from two cents to three. How many cents did it take from the Canadian taxpayer to pay that fabulous expenditure of $32,000? Three million two hundred thousand cents. Sir, it is incredible. I am sure the Minister of Public Works is ashamed of it. I am sure advantage has been taken of his good faith; he has been deceived. May I ask the hon. gentleman if he will explain that expenditure? Many expenditures are necessary and money is not available for them, yet there is waste and extravagance of that kind, taking rocks from a small stream to put them on the shores of an island in order to beautify it when that island is the property of a private individual. Then when the population is outraged by that way of spending money the rocks and boulders are taken and thrown into the water, making a double expenditure in order that nothing should remain in sight of such a scandal. Will the hon. gentleman explain that?

speechtext:
I speak from
recollection and without having the file before me. This was a scheme for dredging the Du Chene river-

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: A scheme all right!

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
-through the village of St. Eustache. I think the dredging extended a mile or more, and the effect was to improve very much the conditions for that village and its residents. As my hon. friend states, the water was shallow in some places and the dredging was to deepen the channel, making navigation better and improving the flow of water past the village, it having become stagnant owing to the fact that the stream had filled at the mouth. Now the usual practice in such matters, where dredging is carried on in a stream of this kind, is to place the spoil along the shore and on the land adjoining. I believe that was the course adopted in this case; the spoil was placed along the side of the channel or lands of the different owners. My hon. friend says that some of the land was owned by the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve). That may be so, but the same method was adopted of disposing of the spoil as in the case of the other owners and as is usual in cases of this kind. It was a scheme for the dredging of this river to improve it for navigation and for the benefit of the village, and not for the benefit of the Postmaster General. If the spoil was placed on his land or around this island it was merely following the same course as was adopted with respect to all the other owners in the same area. I do not know the quantity of the spoil; that is a detail for the engineers. I do not think there was anything irregular or improper in the way the work was carried out or the method employed for disposal of the spoil. I do not know anything about the boulders of which my hon. friend speaks, and I do not know whether it was an improvement or a detriment to the land upon which the spoil was placed. All we ever do is to get the approval or consent of the owners of adjoining land so that there will be no
Victoria Day

claim for damages, because in carrying on the work of the department we have found that if you dredge and put the spoil on adjoining lands there is generally a claim for damages-

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: May I ask a question?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
-or for interruption of access to the water. To avoid that sort of thing we generally get, as I have said, the consent of the owner to place the spoil upon his land, or a release from damage claims. I can only say that as far as I know the usual and regular course that has been followed in similar work was followed in this case.
I move that the committee rise.
